summary: Once-daily SNRI for major depression. Often felt as more “get-up-and-go” than sedating, but nausea, sweating, sexual side effects, and blood pressure/heart rate bumps can show up—especially early.
description: Fetzima is an SNRI antidepressant used for major depressive disorder (MDD). It’s taken once daily as an extended-release capsule that you swallow whole. Some people notice early shifts in energy and focus within 1–2 weeks, with fuller mood improvement building over 4–6 weeks. Biggest watch-outs: the antidepressant warning about suicidal thoughts in people 24 and under, serotonin syndrome risk with other medicines that raise serotonin, higher blood pressure and heart rate, trouble starting or emptying your bladder when peeing, low blood sodium (especially in older adults), and discontinuation symptoms if stopped suddenly.
patient_summary: Fetzima is a once-daily antidepressant for MDD. You swallow the capsule whole (don’t crush or open it). Early changes can show up in 1–2 weeks, but real depression relief usually builds over 4–6 weeks. Common issues: nausea, sweating, constipation, sexual side effects, and sometimes higher blood pressure or a faster heart rate. It carries the standard antidepressant warning about increased suicidal thoughts/behavior in people 24 and under. Don’t mix it with MAOIs, and don’t stop suddenly—taper if you’ve been on it for a few weeks or longer.

primary.context: FDA-labeled for major depressive disorder. Early effects may show up in 1–2 weeks, with continued improvement through 4–6 weeks.

secondary.context: Not a separate FDA-approved use, but in real life, anxiety, agitation, insomnia, and panic symptoms often come along with depression. If those symptoms get stronger after starting or changing the dose, tell your prescriber quickly so they can check for over-activation, a strong inner restlessness (akathisia), bipolar spectrum illness, or new suicidal thoughts.

therapeutic_response.display: Depression: initial effects may be observed within 1 to 2 weeks; continued improvements through 4 to 6 weeks

common_adverse_effects.notes: This is one of the most common early side effects. If nausea is mild, it often settles. If it’s severe (can’t eat, can’t hydrate, vomiting repeatedly), reach out—don’t just white-knuckle it.
Lightheadedness when standing can happen. Hydration helps, but persistent dizziness, fainting, or falls need evaluation—especially if you’re also noticing heart rate or blood pressure changes.
Sweating can be annoying and surprisingly intense. If sweating comes with confusion, fever, tremor, or diarrhea, think serotonin syndrome and seek urgent care.
Constipation is common with SNRIs. If you’re going days without a bowel movement or you have severe abdominal pain, don’t ignore it.
A faster heart rate can occur. This is one reason blood pressure and pulse checks are part of routine monitoring.
Feeling your heartbeat more strongly can happen. If you have chest pain, fainting, or a known arrhythmia, take this seriously and get evaluated.
Even small sustained increases matter over time. If your readings stay elevated, your prescriber may adjust the dose or switch medications.
If vomiting is persistent, that can spiral into dehydration and dizziness. Contact your prescriber.
If it’s harder to start peeing, or you feel like you can’t fully empty your bladder, tell your clinician. If you can’t urinate at all, that’s urgent.
Sexual side effects can affect desire, arousal, and orgasm. They’re treatable, adjustable, and discussable—bring it up.

serious_risks.risk: Suicidal ideation or suicidal tendencies: frequency not defined; risk is emphasized in the boxed warning for people 24 and under and during early treatment or dose changes

Serotonin syndrome (too much serotonin): potentially life-threatening; more likely with other medicines that raise serotonin or MAOIs; symptoms can include agitation, hallucinations or confusion, unstable heart rate and blood pressure, tremor, stiffness or muscle jerks, stomach upset, and seizures. Get urgent help.
Severe hypertension, sustained tachycardia, or syncope: requires evaluation and possible dose reduction or discontinuation
Mania/hypomania activation in vulnerable patients (bipolar spectrum risk)
Low blood sodium (hyponatremia), rare but potentially severe: confusion, headache, weakness, seizures—higher risk in older adults and people on water pills (diuretics)

safety.black_box_warning: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies. These studies did not show an increase in the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior with antidepressant use in patients older than 24 years; there was a reduction in risk with antidepressant use in patients 65 years and older.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Suicidal thoughts and worsening mood: watched closely at every age when starting treatment and during dose changes, with extra attention in people 24 and under

Feeling over-activated: watch for agitation, irritability, panic attacks, insomnia, impulsivity, a strong inner restlessness (akathisia), hypomania or mania—especially early or after dose changes; if this happens, you may be checked for bipolar disorder

Blood pressure and heart rate: checked before starting and from time to time after that; if blood pressure stays high or your heartbeat stays fast, the dose may be lowered or the medicine slowly stopped

Signs of serotonin syndrome when combined with other medicines that raise serotonin: confusion or changes in thinking, unstable heart rate and blood pressure, muscle twitching or stiffness, stomach upset, seizures
Serum sodium in at-risk populations (older adults, diuretic use, volume depletion) and when initiating or adjusting dose
Renal function for dosing limits (maximum dose depends on CrCl; ESRD use not recommended)
Urinary hesitancy/retention: ask directly about urinary symptoms; urgent evaluation if inability to urinate
Sexual function: assess baseline and follow-up (libido, arousal, orgasm, erectile/ejaculatory function)

Eye risk: eye-pressure checks may be considered if your eye pressure is already high or you are at risk of narrow-angle glaucoma; know the signs of a sudden glaucoma attack (eye pain, vision changes, swelling or redness around the eye)
Bleeding risk: monitor for bruising, nosebleeds, GI bleeding—especially with NSAIDs/anticoagulants/antiplatelets
Discontinuation symptoms if doses are missed or the medication is stopped: dizziness, GI symptoms, irritability, sleep disturbances, “electric shock” sensations, mood lability—adjust taper if needed

special_populations.pregnancy: SNRIs are not usually the first choice if you are planning pregnancy and have not been treated before, but if your current medicine is working well you may continue it when planning pregnancy unless there is a specific reason not to. Evidence for some risks is weak, but SNRI use has been linked to a possible higher risk of preeclampsia and miscarriage. Use late in pregnancy can be linked to short-term symptoms in the newborn (neonatal adaptation syndrome, often gone within 2 weeks) and a rare lung-circulation problem (persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn); lowering or stopping the dose before delivery just to reduce newborn symptoms is not recommended. Use the lowest dose that works, of one medicine when possible, have your symptoms checked monthly during pregnancy, and make decisions together with your prescriber.
special_populations.lactation: It is not known if levomilnacipran is present in breast milk. If used while breastfeeding, monitor the infant for agitation, irritability, poor feeding, and poor weight gain. The decision should balance infant exposure risk, breastfeeding benefits, and maternal treatment benefits.
special_populations.pediatric: Not FDA-approved for children and teens. The boxed warning highlights a higher risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies.
special_populations.geriatric: Use adult dosing, but with caution. The Beers Criteria list SNRIs (including levomilnacipran) as needing caution in adults 65 and older because of the risk of low blood sodium (hyponatremia). Sodium should be checked closely when starting or changing the dose, especially with water pills (diuretics), eating or drinking little, or low body fluids.
special_populations.renal_impairment: Dose limits by kidney function (CrCl): ≥60 mL/minute: no adjustment necessary. 30 to 59 mL/minute: maximum 80 mg once daily. 15 to 29 mL/minute: maximum 40 mg once daily. End-stage renal disease (ESRD): use is not recommended.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: No dose adjustment is needed for adults with liver problems.

pharmacokinetics.food_effect: May be administered with or without food

dosing.titration: Fetzima is taken once daily as an extended-release capsule. The standard start is 20 mg daily for 2 days, then 40 mg daily. Dose increases are made in steps, based on response and side effects. Kidney function matters for the maximum dose.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: If you’ve been on Fetzima for a few weeks or longer, don’t stop abruptly. Tapering helps minimize withdrawal symptoms and gives you a chance to catch relapse early.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Fetzima is used to treat {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:major depressive disorder (MDD)}. This is a daily, extended-release SNRI—meaning it’s designed to give steady coverage across the day, not a quick “as needed” effect. You may notice early shifts (energy, motivation, focus) within 1–2 weeks, but the fuller depression response usually takes 4–6 weeks.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)}: Depressed mood, low motivation, low energy, impaired focus, and loss of interest that persist and impact daily function

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: I wasn’t suddenly happy, but I was less stuck. Like I could actually start things.
My brain felt a little more “online.” Still depressed, just not glued to the couch.
I had more energy—but it came with jittery edges at first.
items.note: If activation turns into agitation, insomnia, panic-y energy, or impulsivity, that can be a red flag—especially early on or after a dose change.

items.category: GI stuff (nausea is the classic one)
quotes: The nausea was loud the first week, then it chilled out.
I had that sour-stomach feeling after my dose for a while.
Eating a little something helped, even though it says food doesn’t matter.
items.note: Nausea is very common. If you can’t keep food down, that’s not normal-adjustment; that’s a message to your prescriber.

quotes: I sweat more—like, weirdly more—especially at night.
I felt flushed and clammy sometimes, even when I wasn’t anxious.
My body ran warmer than usual.
Everything worked, but the finish line took forever.
My libido dipped and it wasn’t subtle.
It helped my mood but messed with orgasms.
items.note: Sexual dysfunction can happen with SNRIs. It’s real, it’s common, and it’s worth addressing—not suffering in silence.

quotes: I could feel my heart thump more when I climbed stairs.
My pulse was higher than usual for a while.
I didn’t “feel” anything, but my blood pressure readings went up.
items.note: This medication can raise blood pressure and heart rate. Monitoring isn’t optional—especially if you already have hypertension, arrhythmias, or heart disease.

quotes: I missed a couple days and felt like my brain got zapped.
I got dizzy, nauseous, and irritable out of nowhere.
It felt like the flu plus anxiety—until I restarted and tapered properly.
items.note: Discontinuation symptoms are more likely with abrupt stops, longer treatment duration, and higher doses. Tapering matters.

sections.intro: Here’s what patients commonly describe—real-life, not brochure-life. Everyone’s different, but patterns show up:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Fetzima isn’t a same-day mood flip. It’s a steady build.
key_points: 1–2 weeks: Early effects may start to show (often energy, drive, concentration before mood fully lifts)
4–6 weeks: Continued improvements typically accumulate across this window
6–8 hours: Time to peak concentration after a dose
Once daily: Extended-release design supports daily dosing at about the same time each day

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: With antidepressants, the biggest trap is expecting a dramatic overnight change. With Fetzima, early shifts can show up within 1–2 weeks, but meaningful depression improvement typically keeps building through 4–6 weeks. If you’re getting worse—more agitated, more impulsive, more suicidal—especially early on or around dose changes, that’s a safety signal and needs immediate clinical attention.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve been on Fetzima for a few weeks or longer, don’t stop abruptly. Tapering helps minimize withdrawal symptoms and gives you a chance to catch relapse early.
key_points: If treatment lasted ≥4 weeks: taper gradually over 2 to 4 weeks to reduce withdrawal symptoms and detect returning depression
If treatment lasted 2 to 3 weeks: taper over 1 to 2 weeks may be reasonable
If treatment lasted <2 weeks: taper is often not necessary (but individual sensitivity varies)
Go slower (around 4 weeks or more) if you’ve had withdrawal symptoms before or you’re on higher doses
If withdrawal becomes intolerable: return to the prior dose and taper more gradually
Some patients on long-term treatment (>6 months), especially those with a history of discontinuation syndrome, may do best with very slow tapers (>3 months)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Levomilnacipran is a serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI). In plain terms: it increases levels of serotonin and norepinephrine signaling in the brain by blocking their reuptake, which can improve depressive symptoms over time.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Fetzima is a once-daily SNRI option for major depressive disorder. It may be considered when depression includes low energy, low drive, and trouble focusing—keeping in mind that SNRIs can raise blood pressure and heart rate and can cause discontinuation symptoms if stopped suddenly. It is not approved for children and teens, and you should be checked for bipolar disorder before starting an antidepressant to lower the risk of antidepressant-triggered mania or hypomania.

faqs.a: Fetzima (levomilnacipran) is used to treat major depressive disorder (MDD). It’s a once-daily SNRI antidepressant in an extended-release capsule.
Take it by mouth once daily at about the same time each day, with or without food. Swallow the capsule whole—don’t open it, chew it, or crush it.

faqs.q: How long does Fetzima take to work?
faqs.a: Early effects may show up within 1–2 weeks, with continued improvement through 4–6 weeks. If you feel worse, more agitated, more impulsive, or more suicidal—especially early on or after dose changes—contact your prescriber right away.

faqs.q: What’s the usual starting dose for Fetzima?
faqs.a: Standard adult dosing starts at 20 mg once daily for 2 days, then increases to 40 mg once daily. If needed, it may be increased in 40 mg steps at intervals of 2 or more days. Maintenance is typically 40 to 120 mg once daily, with a maximum of 120 mg/day—unless kidney function limits the maximum.

faqs.q: Does kidney disease change the maximum dose?
faqs.a: Yes. If CrCl is 30–59 mL/minute, the maximum is 80 mg once daily. If CrCl is 15–29 mL/minute, the maximum is 40 mg once daily. In end-stage renal disease (ESRD), use is not recommended.

faqs.q: Can Fetzima raise blood pressure or heart rate?
faqs.a: Yes. It may increase blood pressure and heart rate. Blood pressure and pulse should be checked before starting and from time to time afterward, and if blood pressure stays high or your heartbeat stays fast, the dose may need to be lowered or the medicine slowly stopped.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: The most common side effects include nausea, sweating, constipation, sexual side effects, dizziness or lightheadedness when standing, and heart effects like a fast heartbeat, palpitations, or high blood pressure.

faqs.q: Can Fetzima cause sexual side effects?
faqs.a: Yes. Sexual dysfunction has been reported with levomilnacipran. In males this can include erectile dysfunction and ejaculatory issues; libido changes and orgasm problems can occur in any gender. If this happens, talk to your prescriber—there are options.

faqs.q: What’s the suicidality warning with antidepressants?
faqs.a: Antidepressants can increase suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults (18–24) in short-term studies. The studies did not show increased risk in adults over 24, and risk was reduced in adults 65 and older. Everyone starting an antidepressant should be monitored closely for worsening depression, suicidality, or unusual behavior changes—especially early on or during dose adjustments.

faqs.q: Can I take Fetzima with an MAOI?
faqs.a: No. You need a gap between them. Wait 14 days after stopping an MAOI before starting Fetzima. After stopping Fetzima, wait 7 days before starting an MAOI. Fetzima also must not be started in someone receiving IV methylene blue.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with Fetzima?
faqs.a: Avoid alcohol with this medicine: alcohol may make the extended-release capsule release the drug too fast.

faqs.q: How do I stop Fetzima without feeling awful?
faqs.a: If you’ve been on it for 4 weeks or more, taper gradually over about 2–4 weeks to minimize discontinuation symptoms and to catch returning depression early. For 2–3 weeks of treatment, taper over 1–2 weeks may be used. If withdrawal symptoms become intolerable, return to the prior dose and taper more slowly. Some people on long-term treatment may need very slow tapers over months.

faqs.q: Is Fetzima approved for kids or teens?
faqs.a: No. Levomilnacipran is not approved for children and teens.

It can. Antidepressants may precipitate mania or hypomania in people with bipolar disorder. That’s why clinicians screen for bipolar symptoms before starting an antidepressant and monitor closely for activation symptoms after starting or changing the dose.
